notes_on_source_material: The Nov 2025 paper analyzed in an earlier run has been removed from this knowledge base (different exam board, structurally different layout). This version covers 8 papers across 3 boards: Nov 2021/2022/2023 and May/June 2019/2022/2023 (all Gauteng Provincial); Nov 2019 (Eastern Cape / national DBE paper); and a June 2024 'Common Test' from KwaZulu-Natal Province. Only Paper 1 was analyzed throughout, since Exponents and Surds is a Paper 1 topic in this curriculum. Two other KZN 'Common Test' papers (June 2021 and June 2022) were checked and excluded entirely - both were confirmed, question by question, to cover only Patterns, Functions, Analytical Geometry, and Trigonometry, with no Exponents/Surds content anywhere. This means the KZN board's mid-year common tests are inconsistent from year to year in whether they test this topic at all - the June 2024 one happens to test it heavily, but 2021 and 2022 did not. A file named 'Grade_11_Mathematics_P1_November_2019.pdf' was also found to contain mismatched content (a Nov 2018 Paper 2 memo, not a Nov 2019 Paper 1 question paper) and was not used; the correct Nov 2019 P1 question paper was subsequently supplied separately.

archetypes.name: Simplify algebraic exponential expression with negative/fractional exponents
archetypes.description: Simplify an expression where an algebraic term (containing a variable) is raised to a negative or fractional index, requiring application of exponent laws (negative index, power of a power, etc.) without a calculator.
archetypes.low_evidence_note: Only 2 examples, but the difference between them is now explained (see marking_pattern.consensus) rather than an open discrepancy. Still worth a 3rd example to confirm the pattern generalises.
command_verbs_used: Simplify WITHOUT the use of a calculator

typical_breakdown: M1: rewrite the numeric coefficients as powers of a common prime base, if they are not already recognisable roots (e.g. 512=2^9, 64=2^6) - only needed when the coefficients aren't perfect squares/cubes
M1: combine the x terms and apply the negative outer index (flip the fraction)
A1: final simplified answer
marking_pattern.consensus: Resolved - not a genuine disagreement. The 2021 example (2 marks) uses coefficients (16, 81) that are perfect squares, so the square root resolves in one direct step. The 2023 example (3 marks) uses coefficients (512, 64) that are not perfect cubes at a glance, so the memo explicitly awards a separate 'prime bases' mark for rewriting them as powers of 2 first. The mark difference tracks a genuine extra step, not inconsistent marking - this archetype has a 2-mark 'clean coefficients' variant and a 3-mark 'coefficients need prime-factorising first' variant. A generator should pick the mark allocation to match which variant it's producing, not treat 2 vs 3 as arbitrary.
marking_pattern.notes: Both examples reward the base-conversion/index-manipulation step before the final answer mark.

archetypes.language_notes: Expression given in a fraction-with-negative-index or brace/bracket form, e.g. {A/B}^(-1/n); instruction stem is always 'Simplify WITHOUT the use of a calculator.'

usage_guidance.rationale: 2 examples from credible final-exam sources - fine to use occasionally, not as a dominant pattern.

archetypes.name: Evaluate numeric expression combining surd and fractional/negative exponent notation
archetypes.description: Simplify an expression that mixes root (radical) notation with negative or fractional exponents, without a calculator, where the difficulty comes from reconciling several different radical/index forms rather than from an algebraic variable.
archetypes.low_evidence_note: Fewer than 3 examples support this archetype and its marking pattern - recommend human review before relying on this pattern.
command_verbs_used: Simplify WITHOUT the use of a calculator
Simplify completely WITHOUT the use of a calculator

typical_breakdown: M1: convert root terms to fractional-exponent or prime-base form
M1: simplify each term
M1: simplify further
A1: final answer
marking_pattern.consensus: both examples are worth 4 marks with a similar 4-step convert-simplify-simplify-answer structure.
marking_pattern.notes: The Nov 2022 example is purely numeric (no variable) and was classified Routine (Level 2); the May/June 2022 example nests a square root, a cube root, and an outer fractional exponent together and was classified Complex (Level 3) - cognitive demand rises with how many radical types are stacked.

archetypes.language_notes: Combines root notation (square root, cube root, fifth root) directly with negative or fractional exponents in the same expression.

usage_guidance.rationale: 2 examples from credible final-exam sources - fine to use occasionally, not as a dominant pattern.

archetypes.name: Simplify exponential expression with variable or large numeric exponent via common-base conversion and factorisation
archetypes.description: Simplify an expression where the exponent is either a variable (e.g. n or x) appearing across terms with different numeric bases, or a large fixed numeric exponent, requiring every term to be rewritten to a common prime base and then factorised or cancelled.
command_verbs_used: Simplify WITHOUT the use of a calculator
Simplify completely WITHOUT the use of a calculator

typical_breakdown: M1: convert all terms to a common prime base (or factor out the smallest shared power)
M1: factorise / cancel common factor
A1: final simplified answer
marking_pattern.consensus: 9 examples now. Most are worth 3-4 marks with a consistent common-base-conversion-then-factorise breakdown. The two KZN 2024 examples are the most elaborate seen in this archetype - one reconciles FIVE different numeric bases (2, 9, 6, 27, 3) in a single expression, the other factors out a very large common power (3^2017) similar to the May/June 2019 example. Marks range 3-4 across the set; the underlying technique (common base, then factor/cancel) is identical throughout.
marking_pattern.notes: The two Nov 2021/2022 examples and the May/June 2023 example were classified Routine (Level 2); the Nov 2023 (algebraic exponent n in a rational expression) and May/June 2022 (very large literal exponents) examples required more integration and were classified Complex (Level 3). May/June 2019 example asks for the answer with positive exponents only (root notation converted to a fourth-root/fractional exponent first) - same core technique as the rest of the archetype.

archetypes.language_notes: Always introduced with a 'Simplify WITHOUT the use of a calculator' stem; algebraic-exponent versions use a variable like n or x in the index itself, while the large-numeric-exponent version uses fixed but unusually large exponents (e.g. 5^2006) to force the same factor-out-the-common-power technique.

usage_guidance.rationale: 9 examples across multiple independent papers/years - safe to draw on freely.

archetypes.name: Solve equation combining a surd and an algebraic/exponential term (isolate, square, reject)
archetypes.description: Solve an equation where a square-root (surd) term is combined with an exponential or algebraic term, requiring the surd to be isolated, both sides squared, the resulting equation solved (usually a quadratic), and any extraneous root rejected by checking it against the original equation.

M1: square both sides
M1: standard/factorised form
A1: answer with explicit rejection of the extraneous root
marking_pattern.consensus: the isolate-square-solve-reject structure is identical across all 6 examples now, spanning 4 of the now-8 papers in this knowledge base. Marks are mostly 4-5, with a consistent pattern of explicitly stating the rejected root.
marking_pattern.notes: All three memos explicitly require the rejected root to be stated (e.g. 'x = 1 (NA)'), not merely omitted.

archetypes.language_notes: The surd is sometimes nested with an exponential term (Nov 2021), sometimes a plain linear expression under the root (both May/June examples: √(5-x)+1=-x and √(2-x)+2=x) - same solving skill regardless of dressing.

archetypes.name: Determine the value of x defined by an infinite (recurring) nested surd
archetypes.description: Given x defined as an infinitely recurring nested square root (x = √(6+√(6+√(6+...)))), first express x² in terms of x by recognising that the expression under the outermost root is itself equal to x, then solve the resulting quadratic and select the valid (positive) root.

Sub-part (b), 4 marks - M1: standard form, M1: factorise, A1: roots, A1: rejection of the negative root
marking_pattern.consensus: single worked example only.
marking_pattern.notes: The conceptual leap of recognising the infinite pattern equals x was classified Complex (Level 3); the follow-on quadratic-solving step was classified Routine (Level 2).

archetypes.language_notes: Split into two explicitly linked sub-questions ('write x² in terms of x' then 'hence determine x') rather than posed as a single instruction.

archetypes.name: Apply Pythagoras' theorem / area formulae to surd-valued side lengths in a geometric figure
archetypes.description: Given a geometric figure (e.g. a rectangle or triangle) with one or more side lengths expressed as surds, apply Pythagoras' theorem and/or an area formula to determine an unknown length or the area, simplifying surd arithmetic (including cross-terms from squaring a binomial surd) throughout, with the final answer left in simplest surd form.
archetypes.low_evidence_note: Fewer than 3 examples support this archetype and its marking pattern - recommend human review before relying on this pattern.

M1: expand and simplify surd arithmetic

marking_pattern.notes: This is the only archetype in the whole topic (across all 5 papers analyzed) that produced a Problem Solving (Level 4) classification - the May/June 2023 triangle-area example requires breaking the problem into constituent parts (find one side, then apply Pythagoras, then apply the area formula) in a way that isn't telegraphed by the question itself.

archetypes.name: Solve exponential equation by factoring out a common power term
archetypes.description: Solve an exponential equation where terms share a base but have exponents differing by a constant (e.g. 3^(x+3) - 3^(x+2) = 486), by factoring out the lowest common power, simplifying the resulting numeric coefficient, and equating to the same base raised to a numeric power to solve directly - without needing a substitution-to-quadratic step.
archetypes.low_evidence_note: Only 2 examples found - recommend human review before relying on this pattern.
command_verbs_used: Solve for x

typical_breakdown: M1: factorise out the common (lowest) power
A1: simplify the numeric coefficient
M1: rewrite the target number as the same prime base raised to a power
A1: equate exponents and solve
marking_pattern.consensus: both examples factor out the lowest common power of the shared base, but the KZN 2024 example is more elaborate (3 terms including one with a negative-exponent factor, vs. 2 terms in the May/June 2019 example) and was classified Complex (Level 3) rather than Routine (Level 2) - record as a difficulty spread within the same technique.
marking_pattern.notes: Distinct from exp_surd_008 (substitution to a quadratic) - here the equation resolves directly to a single linear equation in x once the common power is factored out, with no quadratic step needed.

archetypes.language_notes: Equation written as a difference of two exponential terms with the same base and consecutive/related exponents, set equal to a plain number (e.g. 3^(x+3) - 3^(x+2) = 486).

usage_guidance.rationale: 2 example(s) - use sparingly, not yet corroborated by a second source.

archetypes.name: Solve a direct exponential equation by converting to a common base and equating exponents
archetypes.description: Solve a simple exponential equation of the form a^x = b (a single exponential term equal to a plain number), by rewriting both sides as powers of the same prime base, then equating the exponents directly - no substitution or quadratic step required. Includes the special case where b = 1: since 1 can always be written as a^0 for a valid base a, the equation reduces to setting the exponent expression equal to zero. This is the same underlying skill (common base, equate exponents) with a specific, easily-missed value of b.
command_verbs_used: Solve for x

typical_breakdown: M1: rewrite both sides (or the number 1) with the same base
M1: equate the exponents (setting the exponent to 0 in the b=1 case)
A1: final answer
marking_pattern.consensus: Both examples worth 3 marks with an identical 2-step-then-answer structure. The Nov 2019 example (b=32) is the general case; the KZN 2024 example (b=1, base given as an unspecified variable m) is the special case that trips students up if they don't recall a^0=1 - worth teaching explicitly as a named trap rather than assuming it's obvious from the general rule.
marking_pattern.notes: Previously tracked as two separate archetypes (general case vs. equals-1 case) - merged since they are the same technique, not different skills.

archetypes.language_notes: General case: one side may need rewriting as a base to a negative power (e.g. (1/2)^x) before matching. Equals-1 case: base is often given as a general/unspecified variable rather than a specific number, testing whether the rule is understood to hold for any valid base.

usage_guidance.rationale: 2 example(s) - use sparingly, not yet corroborated by a second source.

style_profile.typical_sequencing: The three Gauteng November papers keep the topic entirely inside a self-contained Question 2 (11-14 marks): 2-3 rising-difficulty 'simplify' sub-questions, then one heavier 'solve'/'verify' sub-question. The Nov 2019 (Eastern Cape/DBE) paper breaks this pattern - like the May/June papers, it seeds one surd equation into Question 1 in addition to a full Question 2 block - so the 'topic lives only in Q2' pattern is specific to the Gauteng November papers, not a general November-sitting rule. The Gauteng May/June papers seed 1-3 topic-relevant sub-questions into Question 1's general 'solve for x' list, alongside a Question 2 block whose size and focus varies by year (2019 light, 2022/2023 much richer, including an infinite-surd problem and a geometry application). The KZN June 2024 Common Test is the richest and most unusual source in the set: it places a linked pair of surd equations (culminating in a 'hence' question) inside Question 1, and dedicates the whole of Question 2 (18 marks) to exponents, including two genuinely novel non-routine items (an equation equal to 1, and an x^x = k equation solved by iterative base-matching) not seen in any Gauteng paper in this sample.
style_profile.scaffolding_pattern: Sub-questions build from mechanical law-application toward multi-step equation solving via one of three now clearly-distinguished techniques for 'equal base, related exponent' equations: substitution to a disguised quadratic (exp_surd_008), factoring out a common power term for a direct linear solve (exp_surd_016), or - for the simplest cases - directly equating exponents after a common-base rewrite (exp_surd_017), including the special case where the equation equals 1 (exp_surd_020). The Gauteng May/June 2022/2023 and KZN June 2024 papers additionally reach into applied or genuinely non-routine territory: infinite recurring surds, geometry applications, a 'hence'-linked pair of nested-radical equations, and an x^x=k equation solved by trial/iterative reasoning. Across all 8 papers, no Level 1 (pure recall) sub-question was found in this topic; three Level 4 (Problem Solving) sub-questions were found, all in the newest two additions (one in May/June 2023's geometry problem, two in the KZN June 2024 common test) - the earlier Gauteng November papers in this sample contain no Level 4 content in this topic at all.
style_profile.notation_conventions: The instruction 'Simplify WITHOUT the use of a calculator' (or 'Simplify completely WITHOUT the use of a calculator') is the fixed stem for every pure-simplification sub-question across all 5 papers. Root notation (√, ∛) and fractional-exponent notation are used interchangeably, sometimes within the same expression. Any solution obtained by squaring must show an explicit rejection statement for extraneous roots in the memo (not a silent drop). Domain-style questions are phrased as 'for which value(s) of x is [expression] real?' rather than 'write down the domain'. Marking guidelines award marks as a short, ordered sequence of ticks (method/setup steps followed by a final answer tick); memos do not label ticks 'M' or 'A' explicitly, but the ordering and function of each tick maps cleanly onto that convention.
style_profile.equation_technique_hierarchy: This topic's exponential-equation archetypes form a natural three-tier hierarchy, useful for sequencing instruction: (1) exp_surd_017 - a single exponential term already equals a number (or 1); rewrite to a common base and equate exponents directly, no combining needed. (2) exp_surd_016 - multiple terms sharing a base must first be combined by factoring out their common (lowest) power before the equation reduces to Tier 1 form. (3) exp_surd_008 - multiple terms sharing a base combine into a disguised quadratic (via a squared or reciprocal exponential term), requiring substitution and quadratic factorisation, usually with a root to reject. Each tier is a genuinely different resolution technique, not a cosmetic variant of the others - exp_surd_020 (equation equal to 1) was previously tracked as a fourth archetype but has been folded into Tier 1 (exp_surd_017) since it is the same technique applied to a specific, easily-missed value of b.

usage_guidance_key.purpose: Every archetype carries a usage_guidance.tier so a downstream generator (or Anne-Marie) can distinguish well-corroborated, safe-to-draw-on patterns from thin or unusually advanced ones, without having to infer this from evidence_count alone (which can be misleading - see exp_surd_014, where a count of 3 is still single-paper).

tiers.core: 3+ examples from independent papers/years. Safe to draw on freely and treat as representative of the topic.
tiers.supplementary: 1-2 examples from credible final-exam sources. Fine to use occasionally; should not dominate a generated assessment.
tiers.rare_enrichment_only: Single example, from a non-final-exam source (e.g. a mid-year Common Test) and/or unusually advanced (Level 4) with no corroboration. Carries an explicit frequency_cap. Intended for optional 'challenge' or 'extension' content only - using these as if they were typical topic coverage risks the generator over-indexing on one test-setter's style.
